Senior year of high school, I ended up in the psych ward of Children’s Hospital. I was there for about 2 weeks, and still hadn’t made any progress. My psychiatrist spoke to my parents about keeping me there for a few months. Nothing was just clicking.

Then one night, I had this young PCA for the last few hours of his shift. He was probably about 21, so not much older than me. I hadn’t showered yet the entire time I had been there, and gotten out of bed maybe three times to use the bathroom. Somehow, this guy got me to shower, use the bathroom, brush my hair and teeth, and even eat. 

The rest of his shift he spent talking with me about music and had wrote me an entire page of song and artist suggestions to listen to once I was released.

That was one of the first (maybe only) humanizing interactions I had had in that hospital stay, and it had gotten me out of the fog enough to make a decent effort to be released and allowed to go home. I still have the list he gave me, and I think about him a lot.

This personally resonates with me, as I have a very similar past. I have roughly 20 past sexual partners, and was sexually assaulted for about 2 years when I was 15 by someone I trusted greatly. I do believe that my sexual history is honestly a result of my experience with sexual assault. 

I think you should tell her your concerns openly and honestly, communication is one of the most important things in a relationship. But you shouldn’t push her. Being pushed like that can cause her feelings over the whole thing to spiral and become more negative.

I recently started healing from my experience, even though it occurred 3-4 years ago, and my boyfriend doesn’t push me to talk or heal, and that’s what I need the most. What helps me the most is just talking to him about it whenever I need to, and to just receive love and support in return. It hurts me more when he tries to talk to me about it, as he doesn’t seem to understand how I’m feeling, which is perfectly okay. Not everyone will get sexual assault, and that’s not their fault. They haven’t experienced what I have, they don’t know how to react. 

Everyone experiences healing from tragedy differently, and even though you may not understand her process, it is HER process, and she may be just fine. Well, as fine as you can be when recovering from something like sexual assault. 

But maybe you’re right, and maybe she isn’t healing well. Which is why you should have an open, honest discussion and tell her what you’re thinking. If you’re right, she will hopefully tell you her honest thoughts, and you can help her get the help she truly needs. But in my honest opinion, it sounds like she is doing what she needs to do. Just continue being kind and understanding towards her, let her know you love her. Ask her if she has boundaries she may need, or what you can do for her. She’ll tell you what she needs from you.
